Question: what's one thing about your city that outsiders always get wrong, and one thing you wish they knew?

Question description: so i've been thinking about this lately because i had a buddy visit from out of town and he had all these assumptions that were just... off lol. like he thought the whole place was dangerous and he'd get mugged the second he stepped out, and then he spent the whole trip complaining about how spread out and car-dependent everything is (fair, honestly). meanwhile the stuff i actually love about it—the little neighborhood spots, the food culture, the way people are genuinely friendly once you get past the surface—he barely noticed. made me realize we all carry weird mental images of places we've never been. so reddit, what's the biggest misconception people have about where you're from, and what's the thing you wish visitors actually understood before they judge it? could be a city, a small town, a whole country, whatever. curious to hear the stories.

Question: What's a lesson from your degree that you use constantly in real life (and what's one thing you paid good money to learn but have literally never used)?

Question description: bit of a long one but I've been thinking about this lately. I did a bachelors in accounting and honestly, half the stuff I learned I use every single day at work, and the other half... let me tell you, I have never once in my life needed to recite the finer details of some obscure tax provision I spent weeks memorizing for an exam. meanwhile the one thing that actually stuck with me was some random lecturer going off-script about how to read a room in a meeting, and I swear that's helped me more than any formula. anyway I'm curious how it went for everyone else, whether you studied something super technical or something completely different. did your degree actually prepare you for what you do now, or did you end up learning everything on the job like it seems like most people do? and for the folks who went into a totally unrelated field, what made you jump? I feel like everyone has that one class or professor that changed how they think, tell me about yours.

Question: What's the weirdest thing you've done to save money that you're actually kinda proud of?

Question description: So I'm an accountant by trade, which means people assume I'm loaded or at least super disciplined with money. Truth is, I make decent money now but I still catch myself doing broke-student habits out of pure reflex. Like last week I found myself debating whether to drive 15 mins to a cheaper petrol station to save like 20 bucks, and my wife just looked at me like I'd lost my mind. It got me thinking—what's the most ridiculous thing you've done to save a buck, and looking back, do you regret it or was it actually genius? Not talking about the usual "make coffee at home" advice, I mean proper unhinged stuff. Curious how far people go depending on where they're at in life.

Question: what's something you used to think was "rich people stuff" until you actually started earning a bit more and realized it's just... normal life now?

Question description: ngl this has been living rent free in my head lately. growing up we were pretty comfortable but not like, *comfortable* comfortable, you know? my parents counted every cent and a "treat" was takeout on a friday. fast forward to now, i've got a decent gig, i'm married, and the other day i caught myself adding avo to my grocery order without even checking the price. and then i had this weird moment of like... am i rich now?? am i that person?? lol. it's not like i'm buying boats or anything, but paying for a proper haircut instead of the cheap spot, or just grabbing coffee out without sweating it — little stuff that felt like a totally different tax bracket when i was younger. it's a mind trip how your definition of "doing okay" quietly shifts as your salary does.

so yeah, curious what yours is. was it a car, a vacation, a gadget, finally saying no to roommates? what was the moment you noticed your money situation had changed and it caught you off guard? and for the folks who are super comfortable now, what still feels like a luxury you refuse to give up? spill, i'm nosy.

Question: what's the most unexpectedly weird or wholesome thing you've learned about people from doing your job?

Question description: so i'm an accountant, right? numbers, spreadsheets, the whole boring stereotype. and honestly most days it is exactly that boring. but the weird part of my job is that you end up seeing people's lives through their finances, and man, people are strange in the best way. like i've had clients who keep a separate little account just for their dogs vet bills, or folks who round every single purchase up to the nearest 10 and donate the difference. one guy had a recurring payment labeled "guilt fund" and i still think about it lol.

it made me realize every job probably gives you this weird little window into human nature that nobody outside the gig would ever guess. so yeah, spill it. what's something about people you only learned because of your work?

input_texts.text: Yeah the dangerous rep is way off. People also think it's dead boring but the little local spots are honestly great. My fiance and I walk the neighbourhood tracks most weekends and it's chill. Wish visitors skipped the assumptions and just explored.

Yeah the rain thing gets old. People picture one grey note and miss the actual vibe. My partner and I walked the lake path last weekend and it was packed, dogs everywhere, coffee stands buzzing. That's the real picture.
the trails round the burbs humble everyone, trust me

Honestly the "basic" stuff is the hard bit. My postgrad taught me to actually read data critically, and I use that most days. Sure, anyone can learn it on the job, but a good lecturer just speeds it up.
Epidemiology basics I use every day, like spotting dodgy stats in headlines. But biostatistics software? Paid a fortune, never opened it since. Funny how the simple stuff sticks.
epi stats, never. talking to people, daily.
Honestly I still wash and reuse zip lock bags, my fiance thinks it's unhinged. Twenty bucks is twenty bucks though, that's a coffee run sorted for the week.
I once walked 40 mins to return a $3 lip balm cause I'd already opened it online. My partner still brings it up at dinner. Zero regrets honestly, that's like half a coffee.
reusing ziploc bags is wild, just grab fewer free ones tbh

rent is brutal rn, feel that. mine was decent coffee beans and actually getting my hair cut properly instead of the cheap place. sounds dumb but it's the little stuff that hits different once you're not counting coins.
Honestly some name brand stuff does slap though. I grabbed the fancy yoghurt once and now the cheap one tastes like sad water. My wallet hates me but whatever, small wins.
proper haircut instead of the cheap spot, no shame
Seen this heaps with health clients, they'll tick "active daily" then admit the walk to the fridge is their cardio. The form version of themselves is always fitter than the real one.

In health consulting you see wild stuff. Had a client who tracked their stress in a spreadsheet colour coded like a traffic light. Green days, red days, whole thing. Honestly kind of genius. People cope in ways you'd never predict.
clients confess weird habits the second I ask about sleep
